item.title: Critical Ruby Heap Overflow Exploit (ruby2shell) Disclosed in String Case Conversion
item.description:
Critical Ruby Heap Overflow Exploit (ruby2shell) Disclosed in String Case Conversion

🔍 Overview

On November 19, 2026, the Ruby programming language team disclosed ruby2shell (CVE-2026-132825), a critical heap buffer overflow vulnerability in how Ruby handles string case conversion. The flaw allows remote code execution in certain scenarios, particularly when processing strings in legacy single-byte encodings like ISO-8859-1 and Windows-1252.

🧩 How it works

The vulnerability arises due to how Ruby processes strings containing special characters, such as the German sharp s (ß). In single-byte encodings, the uppercase form of this character is represented as two bytes (‘SS’ in ASCII), but Ruby’s case conversion logic incorrectly assumes the output will match the input length. When converting case for strings with 21 or more sharp s characters, Ruby writes two bytes but checks for only one, causing a buffer overflow.

In UTF-8, this issue does not occur because the encoding handles multi-byte characters differently, but legacy systems still rely on single-byte encodings.

⚙️ Key details

  • Severity: Critical (Ruby rates it as such).
  • Affected versions: Ruby 3.3.x up to 3.3.13, 3.4.x up to 3.4.12, and 4.0.x up to 4.0.9.
  • Fixed versions: Ruby 3.3.14, 3.4.13, and 4.0.10 (also patching six additional memory safety flaws, some of which can lead to code execution).
  • Exploit paths: Affected by default in Ruby on Rails and classic-style Sinatra applications via HTML forms (GET/POST requests). Other frameworks (Rack, non-classic Sinatra) are not exposed by default.
  • Self-hosted products: Bundled Ruby versions in GitLab, GitHub Enterprise Server, Mastodon, OpenProject, Discourse, and Chatwoot shipped vulnerable versions in their latest releases at disclosure.
  • Cloudflare WAF: Blocks ruby2shell and a related integer overflow (GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px) in both Free and Managed Rulesets, with Block as default action. This is a compensating control, not a replacement for patching.

🚀 Availability

  • Veria Labs reported affected default configurations in Ruby on Rails and classic Sinatra before authentication.
  • Cloudflare WAF updates added rules to block both ruby2shell and GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px.
  • Cloudflare patched its own Ruby-based systems and found no signs of compromise.
  • Scanning for exploits is expected to begin shortly after disclosure.

💡 Why it matters

  • Exploitation risk: The vulnerability can lead to remote code execution, posing a severe threat to systems relying on vulnerable Ruby versions.
  • Patch delays: Upgrading bundled Ruby in self-hosted products or container images can be time-consuming, leaving systems exposed.
  • Legacy encodings: The issue highlights risks in supporting outdated single-byte encodings alongside UTF-8.
  • WAF limitations: While Cloudflare’s WAF reduces exposure, exploits may still bypass it through unmonitored paths.

⚠️ Recommendations

  • Immediate action: Upgrade Ruby to the patched versions (3.3.14, 3.4.13, or 4.0.10) or apply backported fixes in distribution packages.
  • Monitor for scans: Expect increased scanning activity post-disclosure.
  • Verify package versions: Check full package versions against distribution advisories to confirm fixes.
  • Cloudflare WAF: Use as a temporary mitigant while patching, but do not rely solely on it.

📊 Additional vulnerabilities fixed in the same releases:

Vulnerability ID Description Engine Affected
GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px Integer overflow in string case conversion String case conversion
(Five others) Memory safety flaws in Ruby’s regex engine Regular expressions

#security #ruby #heap-overflow #remote-code-execution #vulnerability-patch

Source: How Cloudflare WAF protects against ruby2shell (CVE-2026-132825)

item.title: A2A Java SDK releases client and server support for agent communication
item.description:
A2A Java SDK releases client and server support for agent communication

A new Java library has been released to support the execution of agentic applications as Agent2Agent (A2A) servers. This multi-module Maven library provides both client and server capabilities, enabling A2A agent communication across JSON-RPC, gRPC, and REST transports.

🧩 How it works

The library facilitates agent-to-agent interaction by implementing the A2A Protocol. For gRPC support, the project copies the a2a.proto file from the A2A specification repository into the spec-grpc/ project. The java_package option is adjusted to target the org.a2aproject.sdk.grpc package. Developers can regenerate the gRPC classes by building the module with the command mvn clean install -Dskip.protobuf.generate=false.

⚙️ Key details

  • Language Requirement: Java 17 or later is required.
  • Transport Protocols: Supports JSON-RPC, gRPC, and REST.
  • Licensing: The project is licensed under the Apache 2.0 License.
  • Documentation: Full documentation is available at a2aproject.github.io/a2a-java.

🚀 Availability and Integrations

Developers can add the A2A Java SDK reference server for JSON-RPC to their Maven projects. The SDK includes examples for cross-language integration, such as a Java A2A server communicating with a Python client, and a Java A2A client communicating with a Python server.

Feature Details
OpenTelemetry Available as an optional add-on in the extras folder
JPA-backed task store Available as an optional add-on in the extras folder
Kafka-based replicated queue manager Available as an optional add-on in the extras folder
Vert.x and Android HTTP clients Available as optional add-ons in the extras folder

Integrations with Java runtimes are documented in the Server Integrations section of the reference materials.

#Java #AIagents #A2A #Maven #gRPC

Source: a2aproject/a2a-java

item.title: AI Agents Rewrite Curl in Rust While Original Project Adds 400 Bugfixes
item.description:
AI Agents Rewrite Curl in Rust While Original Project Adds 400 Bugfixes

🔍 Overview

During a period when AI agents converted 185,000 lines of C code into 340,000 lines of Rust code, the actual curl project merged over 300 commits.

⚙️ Key details

The original curl project improved during this timeframe of a little more than three weeks, incorporating:

  • Over 200 bugfixes that the Rust rewrites did not include.
  • Fixes for a few vulnerabilities.
  • An additional 200 bugfixes in the following month, along with maybe a few more vulnerability fixes.

💡 Why it matters

The evidence highlights a comparison between the static output of the AI rewrite and the ongoing maintenance of the source project. The text asks whether these clones will keep up with the actual development pace of the original software.

#curl #Rust #AIagents #SoftwareRewrite #Bugfixes

Source: A quote from Daniel Stenberg

item.title: Chroma v3 Released with Go iter.Seq Support
item.description:
Chroma v3 Released with Go iter.Seq Support

Chroma v3 has been released as a new alpha version, bringing significant changes to its Go implementation and module path.

🔍 Overview

Chroma takes source code and other structured text and converts it into syntax highlighted HTML, ANSI-coloured text, and other formats. It is based heavily on Pygments and includes translators for Pygments lexers and styles.

⚙️ Key details

  • Replaces the custom Iterator type with Go’s built-in iter.Seq[Token]
  • Removes the EOF sentinel
  • Bumps the module path to github.com/alecthomas/chroma/v3

🧩 How it works

  • Lexers convert source text into a stream of tokens
  • Styles specify how token types are mapped to colours
  • Formatters convert tokens and styles into formatted output

🚀 Availability

  • See the v3.0.0-alpha.1 release for migration details
  • Try out various languages and styles on the Chroma Playground
  • An authoritative list of languages and styles can be displayed with chroma --list

#Chroma #Go #Pygments #SyntaxHighlighting

item.title: Rust SDK Adds Stable 2026-07-28 MCP Version with New Features
item.description:
Rust SDK Adds Stable 2026-07-28 MCP Version with New Features

This release brings the stable MCP 2026‑07‑28 specification to the Rust SDK, while remaining fully compatible with the 2025‑11‑25 release and earlier versions.

🔍 Overview

  • The SDK implements the stable MCP 2026-07-28 specification.
  • It remains fully compatible with the 2025-11-25 release and previous versions.

🧩 Features

  • Server discovery & negotiation
  • Transport‑neutral subscriptions
  • Long‑running tasks
  • Response caching
  • Multi‑round‑trip requests
  • Standard HTTP routing headers

⚙️ SDK Structure

  • Repository crates:
    • rmcp: core crate providing the RMCP protocol implementation
    • rmcp‑macros: procedural macro crate for generating RMCP tool implementations
  • Basic dependencies:
    • tokio
    • serde
  • JSON Schema generation (version 2020‑12):
    • schemars

📦 Installation & Setup

  • Add the latest published version: 
    1

    cargo add rmcp --features server
  • Or use the dev channel: 
    1

    cargo add rmcp --features server --git https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/rust-sdk --branch main

🚀 Server and Client Lifecycle

  • serve() uses the legacy MCP lifecycle:
    • The client sends initialize.
    • The server returns negotiated server information.
    • The client sends notifications/initialized.
  • Use ClientServiceExt::serve_with_lifecycle to select another lifecycle explicitly.
  • ClientLifecycleMode::Initialize is equivalent to the existing serve() behavior.
  • Discover startup does not send notifications/initialized; discovery completes startup.
  • Each subsequent request carries its protocol version, client information, and capabilities in _meta.
  • For a server, serve() waits for peer input that establishes the protocol lifecycle, such as initialize from a legacy client.
  • A stdio MCP server is normally launched by an MCP client as a child process.
  • Running the executable alone in a terminal can leave this await pending because no client has sent protocol messages yet.
  • After serve() returns, the service handles messages in the background.
  • You can run other asynchronous work, then use waiting() to wait for shutdown.
  • To cancel during startup, use serve_with_ct().

🛠️ Building a Service

  • Use ServerHandler or ClientHandler to build a service.
  • Await protocol startup, then receive a handle to the running service.

#Rust #MCP #SDK #Async #JSON

Source: modelcontextprotocol/rust-sdk

item.title: BMW Releases TRLC: A Domain-Specific Language for Requirements with Meta-Data
item.description:
BMW Releases TRLC: A Domain-Specific Language for Requirements with Meta-Data

BMW has open-sourced TRLC, a domain-specific language designed for writing and linking requirements with meta-data. The project includes a language reference manual and a pure Python reference implementation focused on pedantic correctness rather than speed. The toolset also features a static analysis tool to identify type and check rule issues.

TRLC supports forward references in specific contexts: a record’s component type may be used before declaration, a tuple field can reference a record type declared later if it’s a record, and record types can be union members. However, certain forward references are disallowed — tuple fields cannot refer to tuples declared later in the file, and record inheritance must follow a declared base type order. Checks cannot use fields of records declared after them.

Python implementations serve multiple purposes: validating other TRLC implementations, validating requirements in CI pipelines, and building tools for HTML rendering, diffing, impact analysis, and traceability. The repository includes tutorials, integration guides, and documentation for the static analysis linter.

The Python implementation requires Python 3.10 to 3.14 and depends on PyVCG and PyPI CVC5 (Linux only, for –verify option). Development support covers environment setup, lexer/parser hierarchy, AST overview, and tool architecture.

#TRLC #RequirementsEngineering #DomainSpecificLanguage #SoftwareTraceability #StaticAnalysis

Source: bmw-software-engineering/trlc

item.title: Nucleoid adds terminal workspace, bare-word syntax, and comment updates
item.description:
Nucleoid adds terminal workspace, bare-word syntax, and comment updates

Nucleoid has updated its developer experience and language syntax with a new full-screen terminal workspace, support for bare-word assignments, and changes to how comments and conditional logic are handled.

🔍 Overview

Nucleoid is a next-generation logic programming language built on structured objects and their relationships, extending the traditional Knowledge Graph. It uses a minimum-token syntax for logic representation and a declarative execution model, eliminating the need for LLMs to manually manage control flow, state propagation, and other imperative constructs.

🧩 How it works

The new interactive interface offers a top-level tab layout, with two tabs reserved for future views. A multiline editor sits at the bottom, featuring autocomplete for keywords, built-ins, and model properties, plus in-session input and result history. Results can be inspected in Text, JSON, or Table formats without re-running the program; arrays of objects render as table rows, while other JSON values display in property/value or index/value views.

Key input behaviors include:

  • Enter inserts a newline.
  • F5 runs the entire editor content.
  • Ctrl-J inserts an automatically indented newline.
  • Tab accepts autocomplete or indents.
  • Ctrl-Space opens suggestions.
  • Ctrl-P / Ctrl-N recalls input while preserving an unfinished draft.
  • F1-F3 switch tabs, F6 changes the result view, and Ctrl-Up / Ctrl-Down select earlier results.
  • Mouse clicks select tabs, views, and results; click/drag edits the cursor/selection, and the wheel scrolls individual panes.
  • Ctrl-C cancels input, Ctrl-Q exits, and .help lists all controls.

⚙️ Key details

  • Assignment Syntax: Assignments can be written as target is value. Quotes are optional around a single word. For example, a is 5 and o.x is "good" are valid. If the value is a bare word that does not match a defined variable, class, function, or built-in, it stores its own text.
  • Conditional Branches: In conditionals like a is A if c else B, a bare word in a branch is read as a variable, class, function, or built-in if it exists; otherwise, it reads as its own text. Parenthesized operands are not treated as words, so a is (A if c else B) requires A and B to be defined.
  • List and Dictionary Items: Inside is values, list items, dictionary values, or named arguments can also be bare words.
  • Comments: Hash (#), double-slash (//), and non-nesting block comments (/* ... */) all work in files and interactive interfaces. Comments take delimiter priority outside literals, meaning // is a comment, not an empty regex (use /(?:)/ for an empty-matching regex). Comments retain newlines and source positions and cannot join tokens or supply indentation. Unclosed block comments report SyntaxError: Unterminated block comment at its opening slash.
  • Plain Mode: Running nucleoid --plain provides a line-oriented interface. Piped stdin or redirected stdout automatically selects this mode. Body lines are prefilled with indentation after the .. prompt, and blank lines submit the block.

🚀 Availability

Install the CLI from crates.io using the command: cargo install nucleoid. The standard nucleoid command opens the full-screen terminal workspace from any directory. File execution and the --json and --graph flags retain their existing behavior. References NUC 76, NUC 93, and NUC 94 document the removal of the --c-style-comments, --is-assignment, and --conditional-words flags, respectively.

#Nucleoid #LogicProgramming #CLI #KnowledgeGraph #Rust

Source: NucleoidAI/Nucleoid

item.title: Proof‑Driven Development introduced with PDD Kit and Verus for Rust
item.description:
Proof‑Driven Development introduced with PDD Kit and Verus for Rust

Proof‑Driven Development (PDD) arrives as a new software‑development paradigm supported by PDD Kit. The toolkit helps teams turn their intent into formal specifications, automatically proves the generated code for every input, and falls back to tests when a proof cannot reach.

🔍 Overview

  • Coding agents can now generate whole features that span tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands of lines of code.
  • Traditional line‑by‑line review does not scale to this output, and tests often only check what the agent built, not what was originally requested.
  • A plan is meant to be the contract between a developer and an agent, but the agent is not forced to obey it, leading to hidden gaps that surface only as bug reports or edge‑case failures.

🧩 How it works

  1. Intent → Formal Spec – PDD Kit works with you to express the parts of your intent that can be formalized as a specification in Verus.
  2. Proof Generation – The kit automatically generates a mathematical proof that the agent’s code satisfies the formal spec for every possible input.
  3. Fallback to Tests – Anything the proof cannot reach (e.g., third‑party cryptography libraries, UI code) is turned into informal specifications and covered by high‑quality unit, end‑to‑end, terminal‑automation, and browser‑automation tests.
  4. TCB Sign‑off – The boundary between proved code and tested code is the Trusted Computing Base (TCB). PDD Kit makes this line explicit and asks the developer to sign off on each piece.
  5. Collaboration Environment – The workflow runs inside GitHub Next’s Chopin, a real‑time, multiplayer planning environment where teams and agents can co‑author a shared document.

⚙️ Key details

  • PDD Kit – the toolkit that drives the Proof‑Driven Development process.
  • Verus – the verifier used today; a proof language for Rust co‑developed by Microsoft Research, Carnegie Mellon University, VMware Research, ETH Zurich, MPI‑SWS, UNSW Sydney, the University of Texas at Austin, the University of Michigan, the University of British Columbia, the University of Wisconsin–Madison, and the Weizmann Institute of Science.
  • Chopin – the planning interface that lets a team and agents iterate on the plan and proposed tests before handing off implementation.
  • Formal verification – a mathematical proof that code satisfies its specification for every input, providing stronger assurance than testing alone.
  • Evidence vs. Proof – a passing test is labeled as evidence; only a verifier‑checked proof guarantees correctness for all inputs.
  • Real‑world case – inside Chopin, PDD Kit was used to formally verify the login logic of Pet Store, a Rust storefront. Verus hardened the code, uncovered existing bugs, and proved the absence of login bugs with respect to the specification.

💡 Why it matters

  • Proofs cover the entire input space, catching bugs that a test suite—no matter how large—might miss.
  • By making the TCB explicit, teams understand exactly which pieces rely on trust and can review them separately.
  • The approach scales to agent‑generated code where traditional code review is infeasible.
  • It bridges the gap between the plan (the contract) and the shipped code, reducing the hidden mismatch that typically appears only after deployment.

📊 Components at a glance

Component Role
PDD Kit Turns intent into formal specs, generates proofs and tests
Verus Verifier that checks Rust code against formal specs
Chopin (GitHub Next) Real‑time, multiplayer planning environment for teams and agents

#ProofDrivenDevelopment #FormalVerification #AIcodingAgents #Rust

Source: Formally verifying agent-written full-stack web apps with PDD Kit - Microsoft Research

item.title: Webframe: Go Tool for Running Web Pages as Programs
item.description:
Webframe: Go Tool for Running Web Pages as Programs

Jeff Lindsay released webframe, a Go project that lets you run a web page like a program. It executes the page in a hidden headless web view, streaming console.log() output to standard output and routing exceptions to standard error.

🔍 Overview

  • Runs any URL or local file as a program.
  • Outputs JavaScript console.log() to stdout.
  • Sends JavaScript exceptions to stderr.
  • Compared to the author’s own shot‑scraper tool, webframe is a much smaller package and does not rely on Playwright.

🧩 How it works

  • Implemented in Go, built on the glaze library.
  • glaze accesses the system‑installed browser engine, so webframe does not bundle its own engine.
  • Supported system browsers:
    Operating System System Browser
    macOS WKWebView
    Linux WebKitGTK
    Windows WebView2

⚙️ Key details

  • Project URL: https://github.com/tractordev/webframe
  • Designed to run headlessly; the browser view is hidden.
  • Provides a lightweight alternative for tasks that traditionally use larger frameworks such as Playwright.

🚀 Evaluation as a sandboxing tool

  • Claude Opus 5.5 was prompted to explore the repository, build exploratory prototypes, and assess webframe’s suitability as a sandboxing environment.
  • The prompt asked the model to “put it through its paces” and evaluate security‑related aspects, though specific outcomes are not detailed in the source.

📡 Evaluation as a scraping tool

  • The same Claude Opus 5.5 prompt also asked the model to evaluate webframe for scraping web pages using patterns similar to the shot‑scraper JavaScript command (see simonw/shot‑scraper on GitHub).
  • The evaluation aimed to compare webframe’s scraping capabilities against the existing shot‑scraper approach, focusing on its minimal footprint and lack of Playwright dependency.

#webframe #Go #WebScraping #Sandboxing

Source: Research: webframe: evaluated as a scraper and a sandbox

item.title: Python 3.15 Released with Lazy Imports and New Sampling Profiler
item.description:
Python 3.15 Released with Lazy Imports and New Sampling Profiler

Python 3.15 has been released, introducing significant updates to import behavior, profiling tools, and language syntax. This release, curated by 3.14 and 3.15 release manager Hugo van Kemenade, focuses on reducing startup costs and improving system insights.

🧩 How it works

Python 3.15 introduces several functional improvements to the standard library and language core:

  • Explicit Lazy Imports (PEP 810): Modules can now be imported using lazy import json or lazy from pathlib import Path. The module is only imported the first time a symbol is used in the code. This feature directly addresses the startup cost of heavy dependencies; for instance, installing plugins using sentence_transformers can add seconds to command invocations without lazy loading.
  • Unpacking in Comprehensions (PEP 798): A new syntax [*sublist for sublist in lists] allows for unpacking within comprehensions. Proposed by Adam Hartz and Erik Demaine, this is an extension of the unpacking syntax introduced in PEP 448.
  • Tachyon Sampling Profiler: A new sampling profiler called Tachyon (available as profiling.sampling) joins the standard library. Unlike tracing profilers, it periodically captures stack traces from running processes, allowing for low-overhead insights into running systems. Users can attach it to an existing process via its PID, such as using sudo uv run --python 3.15 python -m profiling.sampling attach 1234.

⚙️ Key details

The release includes several updates to the SQLite module and existing utilities:

Feature Description
profiling.tracing The new name for the existing cProfile tracing profiler.
blobopen() Efficient mechanism for partial reads and writes of large SQLite BLOB binary values.
create_window_function() Allows creating custom SQLite window functions using a class with step, value, inverse, and finalize methods.
setlimit() / getlimit() Exposes a mechanism for setting SQLite runtime limits from Python.
set_authorizer(None) Provides a method to remove an existing SQLite authorizer.
datetime.UTC An alias for datetime.timezone.utc (originally introduced in 3.11).

🔍 Overview

Performance testing of the 3.15.0rc3 release by Miguel Grinberg shows that speed remains mostly consistent with Python 3.14. However, the experimental JIT demonstrated a 1.2x boost over the standard interpreter in a Fibonacci test, marking a meaningful performance increase for the JIT.

With the arrival of Python 3.15, Python 3.10 (released in 2021) is officially no longer supported. The Tachyon profiler also introduces advanced visualization capabilities, including the ability to produce flame graphs, heat maps, and formats compatible with the Firefox profiler UI.

#Python #Programming #SoftwareDevelopment #Python315

Source: Hello Python 3.15, goodbye 3.10, and now I can use 3.11

item.title: Cloudflare Acquires Deno, Announces End of Deno Runtime Support
item.description:
Cloudflare Acquires Deno, Announces End of Deno Runtime Support

On 9 October 2026 Cloudflare announced it has acquired Deno.

🔍 Overview

  • The Deno team released the first version of celld in August, an open‑source implementation of the Durable Objects pattern from Cloudflare Workers.
  • Cloudflare’s acquisition aims to build on celld to “make workerd self‑hosting a first‑class supported way to build and run apps using the Workers programming model.”

⚙️ Key Details

  • Cloudflare will support the Deno runtime for another year with monthly releases containing bug fixes and security updates.
  • After that year Cloudflare will end its development of the Deno runtime.
  • Deno will remain open source, and others are welcomed to continue its development.

🗣️ Statements from the Deno Creator

  • “It’s a joint decision and I agree with it.”
  • “I’m most invested in its success and have put the most work into it – and I no longer think it’s where I can do the most important work.”
  • “There are some good ideas in Deno and it’s well engineered – but it ultimately is not solving big problems.”
  • “It has been sucked into the gravity well of node compatibility, which forces it to behave exactly as Node does.”
  • “Why reimplement Node? It works. Marginal performance or UX or security benefits are not enough. I’m interested in building powerful new abstractions.”

🧩 celld and the Workers Model

  • celld works remarkably well, depending only on object storage for coordination and persistence.
  • It is described as an entirely new model for server development, not just a slightly different API to interact with the file system or network.

🔐 Permissions System Comparison

Platform Permissions model available Network host allow‑listing
Deno Fine‑grained allow‑list for files, folders, and network hosts Supported
Node.js Permissions added in v20.0.0 (April 2023) and stable in v22.13.0 (Jan 2025) Not supported (network is either on or off)

  • “Claude Haiku 5.5” – 7 Oct 2026
  • “We’re going to need default hard budget caps on pretty much everything” – 3 Oct 2026

item.title: jcode: High-Performance Rust Coding Agent Harness Update
item.description:
jcode: High-Performance Rust Coding Agent Harness Update

The jcode coding agent harness, written in Rust, has received an update that improves performance, resource efficiency, and its update workflow.

🔍 Overview

  • High performance coding agent harness written in Rust.
  • Described as the most RAM-efficient and most intelligent harness.

🛠️ Features

  • Offers Homebrew installation, source builds, and provider setup options.
  • Can be driven via a TUI or terminal commands.

⚙️ Update Mechanics

  • In the TUI, run /update to download the latest stable release in the background and reload while preserving the session.
  • From the terminal, execute jcode update then restart the client.
  • Both commands share the same update policy, also applied to development builds.
  • Updates skip older or equal release versions.
  • For dev builds, the running binary’s Git commit is compared with the release tag; builds ahead of, identical to, or diverged from the release are preserved.
  • If ancestry cannot be verified locally or via GitHub, the update stops to avoid a downgrade.
  • The dev patch includes a commit‑count offset and is not used for release version comparison.
  • Default behavior uses features.update_channel = "stable". An explicit "main" channel opts into source‑branch updates.
  • Use /rebuild or the self-dev build workflow to rebuild a checkout.

item.title: Introduction of xlog CUDA-native Logic Programming Engine
item.description:
Introduction of xlog CUDA-native Logic Programming Engine

xlog is a new CUDA-native logic programming engine that integrates neural perception with deterministic Datalog, probabilistic inference, and epistemic world views using a typed frontend and provider-owned CUDA runtime.

🧩 How it works

Reasoning modes in xlog share device data planes, though their execution boundaries differ:

  • Host-orchestrated: Ordinary Datalog and exact inference.
  • Device-resident: Certified recursive and Monte Carlo sampled cores, which record zero tracked host-device transfers before a bounded terminal receipt.

The probabilistic path enables end-to-end gradients via the following GPU knowledge compilation sequence: Provenance $\rightarrow$ CNF $\rightarrow$ Decision-DNNF $\rightarrow$ exact weighted model counting $\rightarrow$ backward gradients.

A final smoothed circuit is certified against its source formula prior to evaluation or caching.

⚙️ Key details

Feature/Benchmark Result
Circuit caching 2.74x MNIST-addition training speedup
Worst-case-optimal join subsystem 27.96x geometric-mean gain over binary-join baseline
MNIST-addition accuracy 0.9561 (compared to Scallop’s 0.9468)
Exact inference Correctness-equivalent to, but slower than, ProbLog2

💡 Why it matters

Performance and utility tests show varying results across different domains:

  • Graph Processing: In hub-skewed triangle-counting, the Souffle-to-fused-xlog execution-time ratio moves from 0.88x at 150k edges to 5.54x at 1.2M edges. Fused peak device allocations ranged from 85-1,033 MB, while the materializing arm required 3,287-44,979 MB.
  • Video Benchmarking: A proximity predicate trained via symbolic credit replaced hand-set geometry at unchanged held-out accuracy. However, within Event-Calculus rule search, it failed ten-fold cross-validation and did not transfer on a leak-free split.
  • Maritime Corpus: Weighted clauses outperformed crisp selection by 0.065 F1, a result reproduced by one chronological training pass.

#CUDA #Datalog #LogicProgramming #GPU #ProbabilisticInference

Source: XLOG: A CUDA-Native Engine for Neurosymbolic Integration

item.title: Cloudflare Python Workers Reach General Availability
item.description:
Cloudflare Python Workers Reach General Availability

Cloudflare has announced that support for running Python code on its server-side Workers platform is now generally available following a two-year preview period.

💡 Why it matters

Cloudflare states that “Python is now a first-class, fully supported language on the Cloudflare Developer Platform.” This release represents a significant investment in the Python ecosystem.

⚙️ Key details

Cloudflare achieves this functionality by running Python compiled to WebAssembly via Pyodide within its V8-based workerd runtime. Notable limitations include:

  • Multiprocessing is non-functional in the WebAssembly VM.
  • Threading is non-functional in the WebAssembly VM.

🛠️ Development Tools

Developers can utilize the pywrangler tool (packaged as workers-py on PyPI) to run a full local simulation of the Cloudflare stack. This tool executes code using Pyodide in WebAssembly within a 123MB workerd binary.

👥 Credits

The release announcement is credited to Gyeongjae Choi, Dominik Picheta, and Hood Chatham, with Gyeongjae Choi and Hood Chatham identified as Pyodide core maintainers.

#Cloudflare #Python #WebAssembly #Pyodide #Serverless

item.title: Python 3.15 Introduces Soft Deprecation for re.match()
item.description:
Python 3.15 Introduces Soft Deprecation for re.match()

Python 3.15 is introducing the soft deprecation of the re.match() function, marking it as an API that should no longer be used to write new code without a promise or threat of future removal.

⚙️ Key details

Python 3.15 release manager Hugo van Kemenade describes the move to soft deprecate the “venerable but deeply confusing” re.match() function. A clearer alternative has been introduced to reflect how the function anchors at the beginning of a string, but not the end.

🧩 How it works

Depending on the desired outcome, developers can use the following functions:

Function Purpose
re.prefixmatch() The clearer alternative to re.match()
re.search() Match a pattern anywhere in the string
re.fullmatch() Match the entire string
